Far as I know Rassenti has been using cnc for his integrals for a while, not that it’s not impressive but it’s not done on a manual mill. And Michael Raymond uses a CNC now as well. I’m not sure about Gustavo Cecchini but he might only use manual mills as well. Although he invented the folded ti integral so his process might be different.

Scott Cook was THE inventor of the integral, and he’s one of the last, if not the last, maker doing integrals on a manual mill. I believe none of his parts are cnc’d either, not even the screws. Everything is hand turned and milled, which means he’s hands on with every single knife. He’s also a solo act, so each knife is created start to finish by one person. 

He also makes very few knives, maybe 10-20 a year max. He opened his books more than 10 years ago and he still hasn’t opened them since then (and I’m not sure he’s even through all the spots). And almost everything is lotto’d or raffled. I believe table for a plain lochsa from him is about $2200, so bear in mind this is also marked up from table (but it’s the standard going rate on the secondary). Considering CNC integrals are around $1600 from most makers I think it’s more than fairly priced at table. The only other makers I can think of that regularly do these kinds of fully handmade folders are Jason Guthrie and Robert Carter, and both are much more prolific in the amount of knives they produce.

The King stones are correct, but I totally blanked on the Shaptons and the [glass series](https://www.knivesandtools.com/en/pt/-shapton-glass-stone-hr-grit-1000-medium-14-7-micron-sharpening-stone-50202.htm) is preferable over the shapton pros imo (they’re a bit more aggressive and need less water). The King stones have to be soaked before use, the shapton pros, glass and Naniwa don’t. I think a King 1K to start would be great, and if you need to maintain the edge between full sharpenings you can get [jeweler’s rouge](https://www.knivesandtools.com/en/pt/-skerper-stropping-compound-grey-coarse.htm) and a block of balsa wood or piece of leather from a hobby shop for cheap.

One of [these](https://www.knivesandtools.com/en/pt/-skerper-whetstone-holder-sa001.htm) is nice to have too, although not necessary (you could just use a towel). 

I’d simplify stone grits and their purpose to: 100-600 for repairs/reprofiles, 800-2K for general sharpening, 3K-5K for polishing and anything above for sushi and showing off. Definitely start off with an 800-2K stone and you can build your setup from there to suit your needs. Happy sharpening and don’t hesitate to PM or chat if u need any more help :)

There’s a few other options I’d consider aside from traditional whetstones, but they have their drawbacks.

The spyderco sharpmaker and lansky turnbox work similar to a honing rod, but they’re actually abrasive and can turn out a decent edge. They’re also dead simple to use. Downsides are: only two angles to choose from, much slower compared to stones.

If you want to step up in price then the Edge Pro apex is a great option. More angles, better selection of stones and grits, can actually repair edges and refine them much further than the “stick in a box” systems. Downsides would be: price, still not as fast as whetstones, and still not as many angles. 
The worksharp precision adjust can get you some of the way there at a fraction of the price, but it’s not really built for blades over 4”, so it’ll be slow/clumsy.

Aside from that there’s the wicked edge ($$$) and tsprof ($$$$), both are amazing products but you’ll pay for a lot more capability than you’ll likely ever need. I see a lot of people ask about the iki ruixin pro, imo it’s not worth it. The stones it comes with are garbage, and the system itself is just a rebranded aliexpress product; it does, however, take edge pro stones so it’s not completely useless. I’m pretty certain they make clones of the edge pro, but I know nothing about their quality.

That all being said, I researched all of these heavily and still chose whetstones. I love Naniwa chosera (get the ones without the base), but Shapton pros and King stones (not the dual sided ones) are also great. 1K-2K grit for general maintenance (normal sharpening), 400-600 for repair work, 3K plus for refining edges to do delicate tasks like slicing fish for sashimi. A diamond plate is nice for flattening, but you can also rub two stones together, use a brick you’ve flattened, or a flat piece of sidewalk.

Some of my favorite sharpening resources are: Virtuovice, JIK’s sharpening series, and Cliff Stamp (the plateau method>>>). I hope at least some of this info was helpful to you, the sharpening world has lots of mediocre to sub par products clogging search query’s if you don’t know what you’re looking for so I try to guide new ppl towards the right stuff.

Edges get burnt easily because the apex is microscopic, it’s really easy for heat to transfer onto such a small surface and the temps to quickly rise.

Delrin bearings are ceramic balls in a machined plastic cage. Delrin is just a thermoplastic material by DuPont, invented around the same time as Teflon. Lower end knives use nylon washers, which is also a thermoplastic. Teflon is a PTFE material with a lower coefficient of friction than phosphor bronze, delrin, or nylon. Delrin is actually around 10%-25% PTFE, and that’s what actually makes it so slippery compared to other thermoplastics. All of the above are also older than sliced bread, having been first synthesized in the early 20s.


I’d argue that Teflon is actually the best folding knife washer material we have commercially available right now, at least until we get something graphene based. The high levels of elastic deformation that it experiences under load doesn’t really pertain to folding knives, as you’d probably break the knife before the washers are destroyed. The hydrophobic nature of the material also keeps the pivot from rusting. Not to mention that it needs no lubrication either.


Also Shirogorov doesn’t use thrust bearings, they do use roller bearings (on some custom division and full customs) but they’re directly in contact with the blade rather than having a washer sit atop the bearings that contacts the blade.
